name: SambaCry: CVE-2017-7494
short_description: Exploit the SambaCry vulnerability for remote code execution via Samba shares.
description: SambaCry (CVE-2017-7494) is a remote code execution vulnerability in Samba versions 3.5.0 to 4.6.4. It allows uploading a shared library to a writable share, then executing it. Similar to EternalBlue but for Linux Samba.
handler_message:
The deployment server revealed the scope of NIGHTFALL. Now you need the paper trail.

Cerberus executives keep their sensitive files on an internal Samba share at 172.20.0.16. Marcus Webb's private documents. Board meeting minutes. Financial records they never filed.

The share runs a vulnerable Samba version - CVE-2017-7494. SambaCry. Upload a malicious library, execute it remotely.

If there's a smoking gun - authorization, wire transfers, the names of everyone involved - it's there.

Get in. Get the evidence.
episode_intro:
SCADA-BRIDGE. That's what they're building. A toolkit designed to compromise industrial control systems across the country.

The deployment server showed you the components. Now you need to understand who authorized this. Who's funding it. Who benefits when the lights go out and people die.

The executive file shares might have those answers. Marcus Webb's private files. The board's internal communications. The money trail.

Somewhere in those documents is the proof that NIGHTFALL is real - and who's behind it.
episode_outro:
Marcus Webb's files tell a story he never intended anyone to read.

Wire transfers to shell companies in the Caymans. Meeting notes with no attendee names - just initials and clearance levels. A map of the United States with infrastructure targets circled in red.

But it's the photographs that stop your blood cold. Surveillance photos. David Chen leaving his apartment. Getting into his car. Entering a coffee shop.

Dated the week before he disappeared.

They were watching him. They knew he was gathering evidence. And then they made him vanish.

You find one more file: a manifest for something called 'SCADA-BRIDGE BUILD-FARM.' An IP address. A distributed compilation infrastructure.

They're not just staging the attack - they're building it at scale. And the build farm might show you exactly what they're creating.

interstitial.title: Episode 4: SHARED SECRETS
interstitial.content:
PREVIOUSLY: The deployment server confirmed everything. NIGHTFALL is real. SCADA-BRIDGE is their weapon. And it's scheduled to launch in 72 hours.

But code doesn't authorize itself. Someone signed off on this. Someone funded it. Someone decided that American lives were acceptable collateral for whatever they're planning.

The answers are in the executive file shares. Marcus Webb's private documents. Board meeting notes. Financial records.

The Samba server is vulnerable to CVE-2017-7494 - SambaCry. Upload a malicious library, execute it remotely.

Time to see what Cerberus leadership has been hiding.

steps.title: Verify SMB is running
steps.narrative: SMB (Server Message Block) runs on ports 139 and 445. Port 445 is direct TCP - the modern approach. Samba is the Linux implementation of the SMB protocol, commonly used for file shares in mixed environments. Cerberus uses it for internal document storage.

steps.title: Enumerate Samba shares
steps.narrative: Before attacking, enumerate what's available. The -L flag lists shares, -N attempts null authentication (no password). Even if anonymous access is disabled, the share names themselves reveal what data exists. Look for anything that sounds like executive documents.
steps.expected: Sharename list with 'data' or similar writable share

steps.title: Start Metasploit
steps.narrative: SambaCry is a serious vulnerability - it allows uploading a shared library to a writable share and then loading it into the Samba process. Remote code execution through a legitimate-looking file operation. Metasploit has a module ready.

steps.title: Search for SambaCry
steps.narrative: The vulnerability's technical name is 'is_known_pipename' - a function in Samba that failed to properly sanitize pipe names. The result: arbitrary shared library loading. It's a direct path from file upload to code execution.

steps.title: Use the exploit
steps.narrative: Load the SambaCry module. This exploit creates a malicious .so file (Linux shared library), uploads it to a writable share, then triggers Samba to load it. When Samba loads your library, your code executes with Samba's privileges.

steps.title: Show options
steps.narrative: Review what the module needs. RHOSTS is the target. SMB_SHARE_NAME is critical - it must be a share where you have write access. Some shares require authentication, which means we need valid credentials.

steps.title: Set target host
steps.narrative: Target the Cerberus file server. This system holds years of executive communications. If NIGHTFALL was approved at the board level, the evidence is here.

steps.title: Set writable share
steps.narrative: The 'data' share accepts uploads. In corporate environments, these shared folders often have looser permissions than they should - people need to collaborate, security gets relaxed. That's the vulnerability you're exploiting.

steps.title: Set SMB username
steps.narrative: The share requires authentication. These credentials were found in David Chen's notes - internal service accounts that Cerberus uses for automated processes. 'sambacry' - an ironic choice of username.

steps.title: Set SMB password
steps.narrative: Service account passwords are often weak - set once and forgotten. 'nosambanocry' probably seemed clever to whoever configured it. Now it's your way in.

steps.title: Run the exploit
steps.narrative: Execution. Metasploit uploads the malicious library, constructs the pipe name that triggers the vulnerability, and catches the callback. Note: Due to a known Metasploit bug, you may not get an interactive session - but the payload executes.
steps.expected: Backdoor service spawned OR 'no session created' (known MSF bug - payload still executes)

steps.title: Verify payload execution
steps.narrative: Since the Metasploit session handler sometimes fails on this exploit, we verify execution through the server logs. 'Module loaded' messages prove your code ran on the target - even if the reverse shell didn't connect properly.
steps.expected: Module '/data/<random>.so' loaded - proves remote code execution!

steps.title: One-command pwn
steps.narrative: After understanding the attack, use the automated script. It handles the exploit chain and verification. Remember: the goal isn't just exploitation - it's finding the evidence of NIGHTFALL authorization.

success_criteria: Logs confirm your payload executed on the Cerberus file server. You have access to executive documents and financial records.
next_steps: Search for PDF documents: find mounted share for *.pdf
Look for financial records: grep -r 'wire transfer' /mnt/
